I recently talked to a founder of a 250-person dev shop who's struggling to win new clients. After hearing his numbers, I could see why:

For context:

This founder's pipeline looks busy on paper:

- Around 300 leads
- Recurring clients adding more developers
- Big contracts that have run for four years

Yet zero new clients signed.

Startups that paid $30k to $50k now vibe code. Mobile apps? "Dead business," he said.

So it came down to one question:

How many new opportunities is he seeing per month?

His answer: "There is no new client we got in the last six months."

That's not a lead problem.

He just lost the buyers who paid for mobile builds.

So here's the shift I recommend instead:

1/ Stop leading with mobile builds and look at where buyers are spending on AI now

2/ Target the non-technical companies that gave everyone ChatGPT and saw no profit

3/ Repackage the capability your team already has, instead of hiring capability you lack

4/ Productize it into a named AI outcome buyers recognize, instead of selling bespoke hours

5/ Build a cold acquisition system so new clients show up before the big contracts end, and scale whatever closes.

See the difference?

You aren't selling hours of mobile builds into a market that moved. Or worse, waiting on referrals that stopped three years ago.

You went where buyers already spend, repackaged the team you have, and sold the outcome.

By the time a big contract ends, the odds your pipeline runs dry are muchhhhh lower.

And that's it.

Hope it's helpful!

PS - I run a free 1-1 Growth Workshop for dev shop founders on repositioning into AI-as-a-service and building a cold acquisition system: https://lnkd.in/gj4Zvb4v

It has felt a little bleak out there of late and so it is nice to be able to see some stats indicating a little bit of positive movement in the market!

This month shows some encouraging signs in the UK jobs market (although the picture isn't quite the same everywhere and that still makes things a little confusing). 

The latest KPMG and REC Report on Jobs shows:
- permanent hiring across the UK increased modestly for the second month running in September
- IT, Technology and Computing leading growth and demand

That's encouraging to see particularly for the technology sector!

Closer to home, the picture across the South of England is a little more cautious:
- Permanent placements falling (although only marginal and I wouldn't say that necessarily echoes what we are seeing)
- Temporary and contract activity has shown modest growth

Whilst there are more candidates available, employers are still reporting shortages in specialist areas such as AI, machine learning, cyber security and software development. I think that's an important distinction. A greater number of people looking for work doesn't necessarily mean the specific skills businesses need are suddenly easier to find. 

For employers - there are opportunities in the current market, particularly if you're clear about the skills you genuinely need and can be a little flexible about the rest.

For candidates - its encouraging to see areas of technology continuing to generate demand, even in a more cautious hiring market.

Its not a dramatic turnaround, but there are some positive signs, and hopefully well see that confidence continue to build over the coming months.

If I lost my entire sales pipeline today and needed 100 verified B2B buyers by next week, I wouldn't waste $5,000 on stale contact databases or spam thousands of people.

I’d open Claude and build the list around a problem, not an industry.

Here’s the framework :

1. FIND THE PAIN

Don’t tell Claude: Find companies in manufacturing.
Tell it: List 10 problems in this industry that can cost a company serious money, time, or lost customers. For each problem, identify who inside the company owns it.
Now you have a buyer profile.

2. BUILD THE ACCOUNT LIST

Give Claude real sources :
• Industry directories
• Company websites
• Annual reports
• Trade publications
• Factory/plant lists
• Public tender information
Ask: Find companies that match this buyer profile. For each one, show the company, location, relevant business activity, why it fits, and the source.

Start with 300–500 accounts.
Then narrow it to the best 100.

3. FIND A REASON TO CONTACT THEM

A company being a good fit is not enough.

Ask Claude to look for recent signals :

• Factory or warehouse expansion
• New contracts
• New leadership
• Hiring
• New product launches
• Regulatory changes
• Supplier problems
Then ask: Which of these companies has a recent event that makes my solution more relevant right now?

This turns a cold list into a list with timing.

4. FIND THE RIGHT PERSON

For every account, identify the person most likely to own the problem.
Depending on the business, that may be:
CEO
Procurement Head
Operations Head
Plant Manager
Supply Chain Head
Then verify the role before you reach out.

5. WRITE THE REASON, NOT THE PITCH

This is where most AI outreach goes wrong.
Don’t ask Claude: Write a cold email.

Ask: Based only on the verified information, write a 60-word message that mentions the specific event or problem, explains why I’m reaching out, and ends with one simple question. No flattery. No buzzwords. No fake claims.

One company.
One reason.
One message.

6. SCORE THE 100
Give every account a simple score:
Fit — /10
Pain — /10
Timing — /10
Value — /10
Access — /10
Now you know who to contact first.

Your final output should look like this:
100 accounts
100 real decision-makers
100 verified buying signals
100 personalised reasons to start a conversation

That’s not a lead list.
That’s a sales system.

And I’d keep one rule :
AI can help you find the evidence.
You still decide whether the opportunity is real.

The goal isn't to send more messages.
It is to find 100 companies with a reason to hear from you.

My contract at Freie Universität Berlin ended on 1 October.

Next, I'm looking for a role as a quantitative researcher, research or insights analyst, or in AI evaluation. Berlin or remote EU.

My last year at FU had two halves. I built an AI coding workflow for a 4-wave panel interview study, and I taught MA seminars in quantitative data analysis.

The research: a language model had to turn about 6,000 answers into data for statistical analysis. My first prompt did everything in one pass. It looked fine on the answers I built it with. Then it met answers it had never seen. It didn't hold up. I split it into 2 passes. One finds the evaluations and quotes the evidence. The other codes 9 variables for each. A validator checks every output. Repeated runs agreed on at least 91.6% of codes for every variable.

The teaching: I built the seminars from scratch, from syllabus and exercises to assessments and final projects in Stata. My students' statistics backgrounds were very mixed. I took them from a research question to results they could interpret and present.

Both halves needed the same thing: knowing what is being measured, checking it, and explaining it to the people who have to use it.

Before FU, I delivered survey research for UNHCR, UNDP, the World Bank and the EU at PMCG in Tbilisi.

India's IT services industry is not shrinking. It is being repriced. NASSCOM projects the technology sector to cross $315 billion in FY26, up 6.1%. The bigger story sits underneath the growth.

For thirty years the model was simple: sell people by the hour, staff projects with a pyramid of juniors, and bill for the effort. AI compresses the effort. NASSCOM's 2026 review says providers are "moving away from FTE delivery to outcome-based, risk-sharing constructs". In Accenture's third quarter of fiscal 2026, managed services revenue of $9.39 billion overtook consulting at $9.33 billion.

If you bill by the hour, making work faster reduces your revenue. That is the trap. Reuters reports TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech and Cognizant tying fees to outcomes as clients demand steep price cuts. Hexaware Technologies's CEO says AI could cut the price of routine projects by 20% to 25%. Everest Group cites productivity gains of 30% to 70% in some services. HFS Research found 40% of organisations expect AI-led services to cost 10% to 30% less, yet only 19% have redesigned how they buy them. Cognizant says fixed-price and outcome-based contracts crossed 50% of its revenue for the first time.

The clearest evidence came from disclosure. Tata Consultancy Services reported about $2.3 billion in annualised AI revenue, HCLTech about $620 million, Infosys about $1 billion, Wipro nothing. All four were de-rated by roughly 35% to 39%. The market was not paying for the AI line; it was discounting the billable base underneath it.

There is a reason for that. AI revenue has no standard definition, and GAAP does not define it either. Companies choose what to include, so the numbers are hard to compare. Accenture stopped separately disclosing advanced AI bookings and revenue from Q1 FY26. nasscom estimates AI revenue across IT services at $10 to $12 billion in FY26, about 5% to 6% of average company revenue.

The mid-tier is winning. Coforge grew 29.2% in FY26, with 86% of revenue from AI-led services. Persistent Systems grew 38.4% in Q1 FY27. LTIMindtree managed 8.3%. HFS Research puts it down to agility: mid-tier firms are less weighed down by legacy transformation programmes.

The change that outlasts the share prices is in hiring. Xpheno data shows fresher hiring fell from about 600,000 in FY22 to roughly 120,000 in FY25, an 80% decline. EY estimates entry-level IT roles are down 20% to 25% on automation. Freshers are now about 15% of hiring, down from nearly 28%. Quess Corp Limited puts the AI and data skills gap across India's GCC ecosystem at 38% to 42%.

The firms that re-rate will be the ones that change what they sell, not what they report.

"TCS Q2 Results 2026 LIVE: Net profit rises 4% QoQ to Rs 13,884 crore, IT firm declares dividend of Rs 12 per share"

Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) reported its financial performance for the second quarter ended September 30, 2026. TCS delivered a stable performance driven by operational execution and deal conversions.

Earnings Deep Dive & Financial Analysis

Revenue Growth & Constant Currency Performance
TCS delivered constant currency (CC) revenue growth in the range of 0.5%–0.8% QoQ. On a year-on-year basis, reported rupee revenue surged 11.2% to ₹73,188 crore, boosted by favorable cross-currency movements as the Indian Rupee traded near ₹97 per USD. 

Operating Margins & Cost Management
Operating margins (EBIT) expanded sequentially to 24.3%. Margin resilience was driven by: 

Operational Efficiencies: Realignment of project delivery models and higher deployment of automation and Generative AI workflows.

Easing Wage Pressures: Stabilization of hiring costs and optimized sub-
contractor expenses.

Currency Tailwinds: Depreciating domestic currency against key client currencies (USD, EUR, GBP).

Capital Allocation & Shareholder Returns
Second Interim Dividend: The Board approved an interim payout of ₹12 per equity share.
Record Date: Fixed for Wednesday, October 14, 2026. 
Dividend Yield: Over the past four quarters, TCS has maintained a total payout ratio exceeding 80% of net income, offering an effective dividend yield of ~5.0%

Share Market Perspective & Valuation

YTD Underperformance & De-rating
Stock Performance: TCS shares traded around ₹2,136 on earnings day, down nearly 35% YTD from its 52-week high of ₹3,336.70. 
Factors Driving Sell-off: Broad-based tech headwinds, macro uncertainty, reduced discretionary spending in Western markets, and fears that AI productivity tools could compress traditional time-and-materials IT contracts.

Valuation Multiples
Price-to-Earnings (P/E): TCS currently trades at ~13.8x–14.0x FY27 estimated earnings, well below its 5-year historical average of 25x–28x.
Risk-Reward Balance: The stock's current valuation provides a solid margin of safety, backed by a ~5% dividend yield, stable operating cash flow, and zero net debt.

Summary Recommendation
TCS remains a defensive core holding. While revenue growth has moderated compared to previous cycles, the combination of 24%+ EBIT margins, strong order inflow ($9.5B–$10B), and 14x P/E valuation makes the stock attractive for long-term value and income investors.

Three in a row: Midlands hiring hits its fastest pace since November 2022 

The latest KPMG and REC UK Report on Midlands IT Jobs is out, and the key findings are:

• Permanent placements up again (index: 52.1). Only the North grew faster. 
• Temp billings rebounded strongly (53.8) after two months of decline, well ahead of the UK average 
• Permanent vacancies still falling (45.8), now 28 months in a row, but at the softest rate this year • Candidate availability keeps rising, with redundancies a big factor 
• Permanent starting salaries rose at the fastest pace since February, driven by competition for skilled people and senior hires 

Skills in Short Supply: 
Permanent: Software Developers, Data Engineers, Automation Testers
Contract: AI/ML Developers, Software Developers 

My Take: Fewer vacancies but more placements tells me employers have stopped sitting on roles and are finally committing. The ones moving now are securing people before the market tightens. 

And look at that skills list. Candidate availability is up, yet Software Developers appear in both the permanent and contract shortages. 

More CVs do not mean more of the right CVs. 

I see this every week. 

The volume is there; the quality takes proper qualifying to find. 

This is exactly why partnership matters. When a role goes out to five agencies at once, it becomes a race to send CVs first, not a search for the best person. 

Give one good recruiter exclusivity and a realistic timeframe, and they can actually do the job properly: understanding your team and culture, headhunting the people who aren't applying, and qualifying every candidate thoroughly before anyone lands in your inbox. 

You get a shorter, stronger shortlist, candidates who feel genuinely valued from the first conversation, and a far better chance of the right hire sticking around.

For IT professionals, salaries are moving again, especially at senior level. If you've been holding off because the market felt flat, that picture is starting to change. 

With the Autumn Budget around the corner, the next few months will tell us whether this is the start of a genuine recovery. I'm cautiously optimistic.

Is confidence coming back where you are?

Something happened recently that genuinely rattled me.

I came across a group of candidates who, on the surface, looked completely legitimate (and really rather good!).


Spoiler Alert ... They were not!


They had put together around 10 highly relevant CVs, with impressive experience at real companies — the kind of companies that would absolutely have hired for the roles they were applying for. Over phone calls they were able to articulate their experience with clarity, and I was confident there was a real person on the other side!

And then there were the passports. Real-looking photocopies of passports, complete with real-looking contact details from references that made everything seem even more credible. Seemed legit! 

But something still didn't sit quite right. How often do so many fantastic candidates, that are all available to start exactly when the contract begins, and are all looking for exactly the right rates? 

I asked to have a video call with them before their interviews. A real person turned up! This wasn't an AI scam! But they definitely weren't the person whose passport I'd been sent. And bizarrely, several of them appeared to be sitting in the same room as the person before? The same background. The same environment. 

This wasn't just someone exaggerating their experience on a CV. This was a coordinated attempt to create completely fictional candidate profiles — using real companies, convincing documentation and real people to get through the process. 

I've been in this industry for a decade. I've had my fair share of knock-backs. I've had moments where I've questioned myself, my judgement and whether I was good enough. I've had to work hard to build confidence in what I do. And if I'm honest, this really shook me! Not because I was fooled — thankfully, the checks caught it — but because it made me realise just how sophisticated this is becoming. 

We're often told to look out for AI-generated CVs, fake LinkedIn profiles and candidates who aren't quite what they seem. But what happens when the CV is built around real companies, the documentation looks genuine, the contact details appear legitimate, and there's an actual person sitting on the other side of the video call? 

I'd be really interested to hear from other recruiters, hiring managers and talent professionals: Have you come across anything like this? Does anyone know the agenda behind it all?
